ex-406-2.title: Catapult field
ex-406-2.question:
A straight wire carrying current I pointing into the page is placed in the uniform magnetic field between magnetic poles P and Q. The figure shows the resultant field pattern.

(a) What is the direction of the magnetic force acting on the wire?

(b) Is the magnetic field produced by the current clockwise or anticlockwise?

(c) Is P an N-pole or S-pole?
ex-406-2.tips:
Tip

By Fleming’s left-hand rule, the external field (due to magnetic poles) points to the left. Therefore, Q is an N-pole and P is an S-pole. Alternatively, B due to I:

In the resultant field, the field lines are denser below the wire. Therefore, the fields due to I and the magnetic poles point in the same direction (towards left) below the wire.

ex-406-3.title: Finding magnetic force using a current balance
ex-406-3.question:
A student sets up a current balance as shown. When there is no current, the frame is at rest. Assume the rubber tube just touches the electronic balance and the reading of the balance is zero.

Now, a current I flows from X to W. The frame remains at rest. The balance reading is 0.15 g.

(a) Determine the direction of magnetic force F acting on WX.

(b) Find the normal reaction R acting on YZ by the balance.

(c) Find F.

(d) How will the balance reading change if F doubles?
ex-406-3.answer:
(a) Upwards

(b) R = 0.15 × 10–3 × 9.81 = 1.47 × 10–3 N

(c) Since the frame remains at rest, by taking moment about P,

F × 0.16 = R × 0.24

F × 0.16 = (1.47 × 10–3) × 0.24

F = 2.21 × 10–3 N

(d) Since F ∝ R ∝ balance reading,

the balance reading will double if F doubles. Exercise 6.1 Q4 (p.233)

ex-406-4.title: Calculating magnetic force on a rod
ex-406-4.question: A conducting rod of length 0.15 m is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.001 T. Given that a current of 0.2 A passes through the rod, find the magnitude F of the magnetic force acting on the rod in each of the following cases.
ex-406-4.answer:
(a) F = BIl = 0.001 × 0.2 × 0.15 = 3 × 10–5 N

(b) F = 3 × 10–5 N

(c) F = BIl sin θ = 3 × 10–5 × sin 30° = 1.5 × 10–5 N
ex-406-4.tips:
Tip

The rod (current) is still perpendicular to the magnetic field, so the answer is the same as (a).

ex-406-5.title: Calculating the turning effect on a coil
ex-406-5.question:
A coil of N turns and an area of A (= l × D) is placed in a uniform magnetic

field B (Fig a). The axis of rotation of the coil is perpendicular to B. The current flowing through the coil is I. Suppose the normal of the coil makes an angle ϕ to B (Fig b). The forces acting on WX and YZ has the same magnitude F.

(a) Draw in Figure b the directions of the magnetic forces acting on side WX and YZ.

(b) Find F.

(c) Find the total moment acting on the coil.

(d) How does the total moment change when ϕ decreases?
ex-406-5.answer:
(a)

(b) F = BIl × N = BIlN

(c) Take moment about the axis of rotation. By τ = Fd⊥,

total moment = (F × D2 sin ϕ) × 2

= (BIlN) × D sin ϕ

= BI(Dl)N sin ϕ

= BIAN sin ϕ (clockwise)

(d) Decreases
ex-406-5.tips:
Tip

a = 90° − ϕ

b =180° − 90° − a = ϕ

d⊥ = D2 sin b = D2 sin ϕ

ex-406-6.title: A simple d.c. motor
ex-406-6.question:
In a simple motor, the coil rotates in a uniform magnetic field.

(a) When the coil rotates,

(i) how does the force acting on side YZ change;

(ii) how does the moment acting on the coil change?

(b) State three methods to increase the turning speed of this motor.
ex-406-6.answer:
(a) (i) The direction of the force reverses every time the coil shoots pass the vertical position.

The magnitude of the force remains unchanged.

(ii) The direction of the moment remains unchanged.

The magnitude of the moment is the maximum when the coil is horizontal. It decreases when the coil rotates and becomes zero when the coil is vertical.

(b) Increase the number of turns of the coil. / Increase the area of the coil. / Increase the current flowing through the coil. / Use a stronger magnet.
ex-406-6.tips:
Tip

By F = BIl sin θ, since B, I

and l are all constant and θ is always 90°, the magnitude of F is constant.

Tip

From Example 5 (p.235),

τ = BIAN sin ϕ

When the coil is horizonal,

ϕ = 90° and τ is max.

When the coil is vertical, ϕ = 0°

and τ = 0.

Tip

By τ = BIAN sin ϕ, the turning

effect of a motor increases when B, I, A or N increases.

ex-406-7.title:  HKDSE 2019 Paper 1A Q27 A simple motor with electromagnets
ex-406-7.question:
A student sets up a motor as shown (Fig a). AB and CD are solenoids connected to an a.c. supply.

Figure b shows how the output voltage V of the a.c. supply varies with time t. Positive voltage indicates that the potential at E is higher than that at F.

(a) From t = 0 to t = 1 min,

(i) what are the polarities of ends B and C of the solenoids?

(ii) how does the coil PQRS move as seen by the student?

(b) From t = 1 min to t = 2 min, are the polarities of ends B and C, and the

motion of the coil the same as that in (a)?

(c) Does the coil rotate continuously if V varies at 50 Hz?
ex-406-7.answer:
(a) (i) B is an S-pole while C is an N-pole.

(ii) It rotates clockwise.

(b) B becomes an N-pole while C becomes an S-pole.

The coil keeps rotating clockwise.

(c) Yes Revision 6 Q10 (p.258)
ex-406-7.tips:
Tip

The current in the coil also reverses, so the direction of rotation of the coil remains the same.

ex-406-8.title: Interaction between two parallel wires
ex-406-8.question:
Two long straight parallel wires X and Y carry currents out of the page. They are 0.1 m apart. The currents in X and Y are 3 A and 2 A respectively.

Take μ0 = 4π × 10–7 T m A–1.

(a) Find the magnetic force per unit length acting on X by Y.

(b) Find the magnetic force per unit length acting on Y by X.
ex-406-8.answer:
(a) Force per unit length = μ0IXIY2πr = (4π × 10–7)(3)(2)2π(0.1) = 1.2 × 10–5 N m–1

Since the currents are in the same direction, the wires attract each other and the force acting on X points to the right.

(b) By Newton’s third law, the force per unit length acting on Y is

1.2 × 10–5 N m–1 (to the left).

ex-406-11.question:
A particle moves in a circular path in a uniform magnetic field at a speed of 0.001c. It has a mass of 6.64 × 10−27 kg and carries a charge of +2e. The strength of the magnetic

field B is 4 mT. Take e = 1.60 × 10−19 C and

c = 3.00 × 108 m s−1. Calculate the radius r

of the circular path.
ex-406-11.answer:
As the magnetic force provides the centripetal force,

By BQv = mv2r,

r = mvBQ = (6.64 × 10−27)(0.001 × 3.00 × 108)(4 × 10−3)(2 × 1.60 × 10−19) = 1.56 m

ex-406-13.title: An electron in a magnetic field and an electric field
ex-406-13.question:
An electron flies horizontally into a uniform magnetic field of 5 × 10−3 T between two parallel metal plates at 2 × 107 m s−1 as shown. The electron carries a charge of −1.60 × 10−19 C. The metal plates are separated by 0.01 m. A voltage is applied across the plates to make the electron travel horizontally between the plates.

(a) Find the direction of the electric field between the plates.

(b) Find the voltage across the two metal plates.

(c) If another electron flies horizontally into the field at a higher speed, how will it be deflected between the metal plates?
ex-406-13.answer:
(a) By Fleming’s left-hand rule, the magnetic force acting on the electron points downwards.

The electric force should point upwards to balance the magnetic force. Therefore, the electric field points downwards.

(b) The magnetic force is balanced by the electric force.

BQv = QE = QVd

V = Bvd = (5 × 10−3)(2 × 107)(0.01) = 1000 V

(c) An electron at a higher speed experiences a larger downward magnetic force but the same upward electric force. Therefore, the electron will be deflected downwards.
ex-406-13.tips:
Tip

Tip

The electric field and the electric force acting on a negative charge are opposite in direction.
